prompt: Heisenberg showed that when light is scattered from an electron to locate it, the momentum transferred to the electron can't be determined exactly, even in principle. What does “even in principle” add?

choices.text: No better instrument or method could remove it
Better instruments could remove it, but none exist yet
choices.why: The limit isn't technical. Even a perfect instrument couldn't say exactly how much momentum was transferred.

choices.text: It holds only when light, not some other probe, is used
choices.why: Light is just the section's example of a way to locate the electron. The uncertainty comes from the wave property of matter, not from the probe.

choices.text: No momentum at all is transferred to the electron
choices.why: Some momentum is transferred when light scatters from the electron; what can't be known is exactly how much.

explanation: The uncertainty is not a flaw of today's equipment. Locating the electron transfers some momentum to it, and how much can't be determined exactly even in principle, which leads to ΔpΔx ≥ ħ/2.

prompt: According to the section, why is there usually significant uncertainty in where a quantum particle is?

choices.text: Its wave isn't localized at one point
Every measuring instrument has some built-in error
choices.why: The section traces the uncertainty to the wave property of matter, not to instrument error: a wave has a finite extent in space.

choices.text: Quantum particles move too fast to follow
choices.why: Speed isn't the reason. A particle's wave has a finite extent in space, so its position is spread out.

choices.text: Its mass is never known exactly
choices.why: Mass isn't the issue. The position is uncertain because the particle's wave spreads over a region of space.

explanation: The uncertainty principle is a consequence of the wave property of matter. A wave has some finite extent in space and generally is not localized at a point, so the position of a quantum particle is usually significantly uncertain.

prompt: In Exercise 9.11.1, a baseball and an electron each move at 91.3 miles per hour, and the standard deviation in the measured speed is 0.1 mile per hour. Which value is the speed uncertainty, Δv?

choices.text: 0.1 mph
91.3 mph
choices.why: 91.3 mph is the speed itself. The uncertainty is the standard deviation of the measured speed, 0.1 mph.

choices.text: 0.2 mph, from 91.2 to 91.4 mph
choices.why: The uncertainty is the standard deviation, 0.1 mph, not the full width from 91.2 to 91.4 mph.

choices.text: 91.4 mph
choices.why: That is the speed plus its standard deviation. Δv is the standard deviation alone, 0.1 mph.

explanation: An uncertainty is a standard deviation, so Δv = 0.1 mph. The speed itself, 91.3 mph, is needed for the wavelengths, but the minimum Δx depends on Δv.

prompt: In Exercise 9.11.1, the standard deviation in the measured speed is 0.1 mile per hour. Using 1 mile per hour = 0.447 m/s, what is this standard deviation in m/s?
explanation: 0.1 × 0.447 m/s = 0.0447 m/s. Speeds must be in SI units before they are used with ħ in J·s.

prompt: In Exercise 9.11.1, the baseball (140 g) and the electron have the same speed uncertainty Δv. Their masses are known exactly, so Δp = mΔv. Which has the larger uncertainty in momentum?

choices.text: The baseball
The electron
choices.why: With the same Δv, Δp = mΔv is larger for the larger mass, and the electron's mass is far smaller.

choices.text: Both the same, since Δv is the same
choices.why: Δp also depends on the mass. With the same Δv, the 140 g baseball has a far larger Δp.

choices.text: Neither, since both speeds are known
choices.why: The speeds are known only to within 0.1 mph, so Δv, and hence Δp, isn't zero.

explanation: Δp = mΔv. With the same Δv, the 0.140 kg baseball, enormously heavier than the electron, has an enormously larger momentum uncertainty.

prompt: In Exercise 9.11.1, the baseball and the electron have the same Δv. Using Δx ≥ ħ/(2mΔv), which has the larger minimum uncertainty in position?

choices.text: The electron, since its mass is far smaller
The baseball, since it is a much bigger object
choices.why: Size isn't in the formula. The minimum Δx = ħ/(2mΔv) is larger for the smaller mass, the electron.

choices.text: Both the same, since they share the same Δv
choices.why: The mass is in the denominator too, so the light electron has a much larger minimum Δx.

choices.text: The baseball, since it has more momentum
choices.why: The momentum itself isn't in the formula, only m and Δv. With the same Δv, the larger mass gives the smaller minimum Δx.

explanation: With the same Δv, the minimum Δx = ħ/(2mΔv) is inversely proportional to the mass. The electron's tiny mass gives it a far larger minimum Δx than the baseball.

prompt: Working Exercise 9.11.1 gives the electron a minimum position uncertainty of about 1.3 mm (1.3 × 10^−3 m). What does this mean?

choices.text: Its position can't be pinned down better than about 1 mm
The electron is about a millimeter across
choices.why: Δx is the uncertainty in where the electron is, not its size.

choices.text: Its position is known more precisely than the baseball's
choices.why: The baseball's minimum Δx is about 8 × 10^−33 m, far smaller. The electron's position is the less certain one.

choices.text: It can't move more than about 1 mm from where it started
choices.why: Δx doesn't limit how far the electron travels. It is the smallest possible uncertainty in where the electron is.

explanation: Δx ≥ ħ/(2mΔv) is a lower limit on the uncertainty in position. For the electron it comes to about 1.3 × 10^−3 m, so its position is uncertain by at least about a millimeter, enormous on the scale of atoms.

prompt: Exercise 9.11.1 gives the baseball and the electron the same speed and the same speed uncertainty. What does this choice let you see?

choices.text: How mass alone changes Δx and the wavelength
That all objects have the same Δx at the same Δv
choices.why: They don't: the minimum Δx = ħ/(2mΔv) depends on the mass, which is the point of the comparison.

choices.text: That the principle holds only at fastball speeds
choices.why: 91.3 mph just gives a familiar speed. The uncertainty principle holds at any speed.

choices.text: That heavier objects have longer wavelengths
choices.why: In λ = h/(mv) the mass is in the denominator, so at the same speed a heavier object has a shorter wavelength.

explanation: With v and Δv the same, only the mass differs. Both the minimum Δx = ħ/(2mΔv) and the wavelength λ = h/(mv) have m in the denominator, so the comparison shows the effect of mass alone.

prompt: In Exercise 9.11.1 the electron moves at 91.3 mph, about 40.8 m/s. Use λ = h/(mv) with h = 6.63 × 10^−34 J·s and m = 9.11 × 10^−31 kg. What is its de Broglie wavelength, in m? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e-19.)
explanation: λ = 6.63 × 10^−34/(9.11 × 10^−31 × 40.8) = 1.78 × 10^−5 m, about 18 μm. Such a slow electron has a very long wavelength.

prompt: In Exercise 9.11.1 the baseball (m = 0.140 kg) and the electron (m = 9.11 × 10^−31 kg) have the same speed. With λ = h/(mv), the ratio λ_electron/λ_baseball equals m_baseball/m_electron. What is this ratio? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e13.)
explanation: 0.140/(9.11 × 10^−31) = 1.54 × 10^29. The electron's wavelength is about 10^29 times the baseball's, and its minimum Δx is larger by the same factor, since both go as 1/m.
